hero.headline: Product strategy for complex software.
hero.subdescription: Before the interface. We map business goals, user needs and system constraints into one direction the whole team can build against.

paragraphs: They fail because six teams held six different ideas of what the product was for, and nobody wrote the difference down. By the time that surfaces it looks like a design problem. It is not.
Strategy work is unglamorous: interviews, timing studies, arguments about scope. It is also the only part of the process that can save you from building the wrong thing well.

items.title: Product discovery
items.body: Stakeholder interviews, existing-system audit, and a written account of what is actually true today rather than what the org believes.

items.title: UX research
items.body: We talk to the people who use the thing. On site where it matters — you learn more in an hour beside someone than a week of survey data.

items.title: Workflow mapping
items.body: Every step, every handoff, timed. This is where the eight-minute problems hiding behind the forty-minute complaint show up.

items.title: Information architecture
items.body: How the product is organised, named and navigated, decided before anyone argues about a menu.

items.title: Roadmap definition
items.body: Scoped and sequenced, with the reasoning attached so it survives the next reprioritisation.

items.title: Success metrics
items.body: What we agree to measure, and the baseline we measure it against. Without a baseline there is no result later.

items: A prioritised opportunity map, with the evidence behind each item
A product direction your engineering and business leads have both signed
Baseline measurements, so the work can be judged honestly afterwards
The research itself — recordings, notes and findings, not just a summary

relatedWork.title: Loan origination redesign
relatedWork.body: Three weeks of shadowing found that 80% of handling time sat in three of six tools. That finding changed the whole engagement.

items.question: Is this worth it if we already know what to build?
items.answer: Sometimes not, and we will say so. But "we know what to build" usually means one person knows. The value is in finding where that belief is not shared.

items.question: How long does it take?
items.answer: Four to six weeks for a focused product. Longer where users are hard to reach or several acquired systems are involved.

items.question: Can this run alongside design?
items.answer: It can, and often should. Discovery that stops the world for two months is rarely worth what it costs.

hero.headline: Enterprise UX and UI design.
hero.subdescription: Interface systems for products that do not get simpler over time — dashboards, complex flows, and the mobile apps that sit beside them.

paragraphs: Anyone can design a good first screen. The problem arrives at screen fifty, designed by someone who never saw the first ten, using values nobody wrote down.
We design the screens and the layer underneath them at the same time, so the product stays coherent after we leave rather than needing a redesign every eighteen months.

items.title: Enterprise dashboards
items.body: Dense, data-heavy interfaces where the job is comprehension under time pressure, not decoration.

items.title: Complex flows
items.body: Multi-step, multi-actor processes with real failure states — partial saves, approvals, things that time out.

items.title: Mobile app design
items.body: iOS and Android, designed against the same tokens as the web product so they do not drift apart.

items.title: Design systems

items.title: Interactive prototypes
items.body: Real enough to test with real users, because a static frame never reveals a broken flow.

items.title: Accessibility review
items.body: WCAG 2.2 AA as a working constraint, not an audit you fail at the end.

items.question: Do you design for developers we do not employ yet?
items.answer: Yes. Systems work best when they assume the team will change. That is most of the point.

items.question: What if we already have a component library?
items.answer: We audit it first. The problem is usually not the components — it is that nothing governs how they get used.

items.question: Do you do brand and marketing design too?
items.answer: No. We design products. A studio that does everything does none of it especially well.

hero.headline: AI product design and automation UX.
hero.subdescription: AI only helps when people trust it. We design the interface layer that makes automated decisions legible, correctable and worth relying on.

paragraphs: Most failed AI features do not fail on accuracy. They fail because the person on the other end could not tell why a decision was made, could not correct it, and stopped looking.
The design problem is not the model. It is confidence, correction and consequence — what the interface shows, what it lets you override, and what happens when it is wrong.

items.title: AI assistants
items.body: Conversational and embedded assistants that show their working instead of asserting an answer.

items.title: Intelligent workflows
items.body: Automation that hands back to a person at the right moment, rather than at the moment it breaks.

items.title: Process automation
items.body: Where the repetitive work actually is, mapped before anything is automated.

items.title: Model output UX
items.body: Confidence, provenance and uncertainty made visible without turning every screen into a dashboard.

items.title: Human-in-the-loop design
items.body: Review and override paths designed as the primary flow, not an escape hatch.

items.title: AI-powered products
items.body: Products where the model is the product, and the interface has to carry the trust.

items: Interface patterns for confidence, provenance and correction
A defined escalation path for when the model is wrong — because it will be
Automation scoped to where it pays, with the rest left alone deliberately

relatedWork.body: An assistant that now resolves 60% of inbound tickets without a human — and hands over cleanly when it should.

items.question: Do you build the model?
items.answer: No. We design everything around it. If you need modelling we will tell you honestly that it is not us.

items.question: Our AI feature launched and nobody uses it. Can you help?
items.answer: That is the common case. Usually the answer is in what the interface never showed the user, not in the model.

items.question: Is this only for chat interfaces?
items.answer: No, and chat is often the wrong shape. Most useful automation is invisible until it needs a decision.

hero.headline: Design systems that survive handoff.
hero.subdescription: Tokens, components and governance shipped into your repository — versioned, documented, and usable by people who were never in the workshop.

paragraphs: A component library is the components. A design system is those components, the tokens underneath them, the rules for adding new ones, and documentation good enough that someone who was not there still makes the right decision.
The difference shows up about a year in. One of them still governs how the product looks. The other has quietly become a folder people copy from.

items.title: Design system audit
items.body: Where you are now, honestly: what exists, what actually gets used, and what gets bypassed. Usually the first thing worth buying.

items.title: Token architecture
items.body: Colour, space, type, radius and motion, structured so brand, theme and density stay independent instead of multiplying.

items.title: Component library
items.body: Built against the states that occur — empty, error, partial, loading — and shipped as code into your repository.

items.title: Governance
items.body: Contribution rules, review workflow, and the tooling that enforces them. Rules held in memory are not rules.

items.title: Multi-brand and theming
items.body: One foundation carrying several brands or themes, without duplicating everything for each.

items.title: Accessibility built in
items.body: WCAG 2.2 AA inside the components, so screens inherit it rather than failing an audit later.

items.question: Do we need a design system yet?
items.answer: If you have one product and two designers, probably not. The tipping point is usually the third team shipping screens nobody else reviews.

items.question: We already have one and it is not working. Can you fix it?
items.answer: That is the common case, and the answer is almost never more components. Start with the audit — the problem is usually governance, not inventory.

items.question: Who maintains it after you leave?
items.answer: Your team. That is the point, and it is why the contribution guide and the governance model matter more than the component count.
